doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Meeting Cannonball Adderley
summary: Why he loves Cannonball's joy, and the story of Cannonball listening from the wings and giving him a thumbs up in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Wow. It sounds like you’re doing really good stuff. Our tape’s going to run out pretty soon. But I wanted to go back. You said the magic word to me early on. I’m a huge Cannonball fan, and always have been. And I wonder, why are you?

It was, I got the feeling of absolute joy when he played. It was life, it was joy, it was come on, let’s do it. And that’s what I tried to bring, rather than just slugging over patterns and things, I wanted to bring some kind of joy to what’s played. And I actually got to meet him before he passed away. We were playing at McCoy Place in Chicago. And I did the ugly fan thing. Said “oh, I’ve copped all your licks and I’ve listened to all your albums.” And he said, “oh, that’s great.” He said, “well I’ve heard you too.” Because he had the “Live at Jimmy’s” album. And so he said, “do you get a solo?” And I said, “yeah, at the end of the set.” And he said, “I’ll be there.” And so I got up to play, got the sprit thing, and all of a sudden in my peripheral vision I noticed Cannonball sliding into the wings. And he stayed there until the end, so he heard the whole thing. And when we were done he wasn’t there anymore. And I ran into him again, he was coming up the hallway, walking with a bunch of reporters. And he just kept on talking but he reached out and gave me the thumbs up.
I was unapproachable for a week. And I was very sad when he died.
Really. Me too. And Nat, and the whole thing, it was just perfect, the way he took soul jazz and infused it with his personality, and the way he talked to the crowd.
Yeah, he was very folksy but a great guy. A former school teacher.
Yup. And that sound you know. I kid my students, I say, “I’m now going to play for you’re the greatest note ever played.” And I play the build-up in “Mercy Mercy” when it goes [scats].
